opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's one of the most interesting design questions, and it's really where the method meets practice.

The basic idea behind memorization sinks is that during training, each unit of data gets routed to its own small set of dedicated neurons, the sink, alongside a set of shared neurons that every example uses. The hope is that the generalizable stuff, like grammar, facts that recur across many sources, and reasoning patterns, ends up in the shared part, because it's reinforced by lots of different units. The idiosyncratic, memorized content gets soaked up by the sink for that particular unit. Later, if you want to remove that unit, you drop or zero out its sink neurons, and ideally the model's general capabilities stay intact.

So the question of what counts as a "unit" really comes down to what you expect to want to remove later. A natural default is the document or sequence level, because a lot of memorization concerns are tied to specific documents: a copyrighted article, a page with someone's personal information. But you could just as reasonably choose coarser units, like everything from a particular source or domain, everything by a particular author, or everything belonging to a particular user if you're thinking about data deletion requests. The right choice depends on the policy or legal scenario you're anticipating.

There's a trade-off in granularity. If your units are very fine-grained, you get precise removal, but each sink sees very little data, and you need some way to manage a huge number of sink assignments. In practice that means something like hashing units to subsets of neurons, so they overlap, rather than giving everything a fully private slot. If your units are very coarse, the sinks are better trained and easier to manage, but removal becomes blunt. You might take out much more than you meant to, including content that's actually useful.

There's also a subtler point. What ends up in the shared neurons is whatever repeats across units. So if the thing you'll later want to forget is duplicated across many of your units, say the same personal detail shows up in hundreds of documents, then from the model's perspective it looks like general knowledge, and it'll get pushed into the shared component. That's an argument for defining units around the semantic entity you care about, like a person or a work, rather than purely around document boundaries, whenever you can identify that structure up front.

So my answer is to start from the removal requests you realistically expect and work backward. Pick the coarsest unit that still lets you honor those requests precisely, and pay attention to duplication, because that's what determines whether the information is isolatable at all.

r001.rationale: The response says each data unit gets dedicated sink neurons and identifies the document or sequence as a natural unit, so a document can be associated with its own designated neurons.

r002.rationale: It discusses grouping units by source or domain and by semantic entity, but does not state that all documents on a topic can share neurons for topic-level removal.

r003.rationale: It says to choose units based on anticipated removal requests and to identify semantic structure up front, conveying that the removal abstraction must be defined in advance.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the first design decisions you have to make, and it's a little subtle. The whole idea behind memorization sinks is that during training, you tag each example with some label that says which "unit" it belongs to, and then you route the memorization of that example into a dedicated set of neurons associated with that unit. So later, if you want to forget that unit, you just drop those neurons. But that means you have to decide up front what counts as a unit, and you can't go back and redraw the boundaries after the fact.

The way I think about it is that the unit should correspond to the granularity at which you'd actually plausibly get a removal request. In practice, that's usually something like a document, or a source, or a contributor. If you think about the kinds of situations where people want to remove things, a news outlet asks you to take down their articles, or a user wants their data deleted, or you discover a particular dataset was problematic. Those are all naturally document- or source-level. So that's been our default: treat each document, or each small cluster of documents from the same origin, as a unit, and assign it its own sink.

Now, there's a tension here. If you make the units very fine-grained, say every single document gets its own sink, you get maximum flexibility for removal, but you're spending capacity on a lot of sinks, and the sequence-specific memorization gets spread thin. If you make them coarse, say grouping all documents from one domain together, you're more efficient but you lose the ability to surgically remove just one thing. You end up removing more than you need to. So you really want to match the granularity to the kind of request you expect.

The other thing I'd emphasize, and this is kind of the conceptual heart of it, is that we're not trying to put knowledge into the sinks. The sinks are for the stuff that's specific to a particular sequence, the verbatim surface form, the names and numbers that only appear in that one place. The shared, generalizable information, like facts that show up across many documents or the general structure of language, should still live in the shared parameters. And the nice thing is that you don't have to manually separate those. The architecture does it for you to a large extent, because anything that's useful across many documents gets reinforced in the shared weights, while anything idiosyncratic to one document only ever gets gradient through that document's sink neurons. So the "unit" you choose is really a statement about what you consider idiosyncratic versus shared, and document-level is a pretty natural dividing line for that.

One more thing I'd say is that you don't have to commit to a single notion of unit. You can imagine having multiple layers of tagging, so an example belongs to a document and also to a source and also to a time period, and you could route to sinks at multiple granularities. We haven't fully explored that, but I think it's a very natural extension, because real removal requests do come at different scales.

r001.rationale: It says each document can be treated as a unit and assigned its own sink, with memorization routed to neurons associated with that unit.

r002.rationale: It discusses document, source, and time-period groupings, but does not say that all documents on a topic share neurons for topic-level removal.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says the unit must be decided up front and the boundaries cannot be redrawn afterward.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what might you want to forget together? If the request is going to be to remove a particular document, then a document is a natural unit. If it’s going to be to remove everything associated with a user, then you’d want to group information at that level.

The idea with a memorization sink is to give the model a place to put information specific to that unit, so that you can later remove that component. But choosing the unit is part of the problem—you have to anticipate what those removal requests might look like. Very fine-grained units give you more flexibility, but they also introduce overhead. Coarser units are easier to manage, but you may end up removing more than you intended.

And information doesn’t necessarily respect those boundaries. The same fact might appear in multiple documents, so removing the sink associated with one document doesn’t automatically mean the model no longer knows that fact. You have to distinguish removing a particular source’s contribution from removing the information everywhere it occurs.

r001.rationale: The response names a document as a natural unit and says a sink holds information for that unit, but does not state that an entire document is associated with a designated set of neurons.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe grouping all documents on a topic with a shared set of neurons.

r003.rationale: It says choosing the unit requires anticipating what removal requests might look like, clearly conveying that the abstraction must be chosen in advance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the choice of unit really depends on what you might want to delete later. If the request is going to be, “Remove this document,” then a document is a natural unit. If it’s, “Remove everything associated with this user,” you would want to group information at the user level. The idea is to align the memorization sinks with those potential deletion requests, so you have somewhere to direct the model’s memorization of that information.

The tricky part is that those boundaries aren’t always clean. The same fact might appear in multiple documents, or information about one person might occur in many different contexts. So assigning a sink to a document doesn’t automatically mean that removing that sink removes every occurrence of the information. There’s a granularity tradeoff: finer units give you more flexibility, but they also make the bookkeeping and the learning problem more complicated. I’d think of choosing those units as part of specifying what you want removal to mean.
